lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 1.

items.signText:
SWIMMING POOL USERS
From 1 June, children under 8 must have an adult with them in the water at all times. Older children may swim on their own but need to show a pool card, which they can get from reception.
items.question: What is the new rule at the swimming pool?
options: a) Children under 8 can get a pool card from reception.
b) Young children may not swim without an adult.
c) All children must swim with an adult at all times.
items.explanation: The notice says 'children under 8 must have an adult with them in the water at all times'. It is not all children, because 'older children may swim on their own', and the pool card is for these older children, not for children under 8.

items.signText: Leo, the tennis courts in the park are fully booked tomorrow, so I've reserved one at the sports centre instead. It's further away, so let's meet at the bus stop at 9.30 rather than 10. Sam
items.question: Why has Sam written to Leo?
options: a) To explain why they need to meet earlier than planned
b) To cancel their game because there are no courts free
c) To ask Leo to book a court at the sports centre
items.explanation: Sam has booked a court at the sports centre, which is 'further away', so Sam suggests meeting 'at 9.30 rather than 10' – earlier than planned. The game is not cancelled, and Sam has already booked the court ('I've reserved one'), so Leo does not need to do it.

items.signText:
YOGA CLASSES
Our Tuesday evening class has become so popular that we have added a second class on Thursdays at the same time. Please book online at least a day before, as places cannot be reserved by phone.
items.question: What is the sports centre telling people?
options: a) The Tuesday yoga class has moved to Thursday.
b) Places in yoga classes can now be booked by phone.
c) There is now an extra yoga class every week.
items.explanation: The centre says 'we have added a second class on Thursdays', so there is one more class each week. The Tuesday class has not moved – the new class is in addition to it – and places 'cannot be reserved by phone'.

items.signText: Dogs are welcome in all areas of the park except the children's playground and the flower garden. Please keep your dog on a lead near the lake between April and July, when birds are nesting.
items.question: What does the sign say about dogs?
options: a) They cannot come into the park between April and July.
b) They must be kept on a lead everywhere in the park.
c) They are not allowed in certain parts of the park.
items.explanation: Dogs are welcome 'in all areas of the park except the children's playground and the flower garden', so there are some parts where they cannot go. Between April and July they can still come in, but must be on a lead only 'near the lake', not everywhere.

items.signText:
PARK CAFÉ
Our kitchen is being repaired this week. Hot meals will not be available until Monday, but you can still buy sandwiches, cold drinks and ice creams at the counter. We are sorry for any inconvenience.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) You can buy cold food this week, but not hot meals.
b) The café is looking for new staff for its kitchen.
c) The café will be completely closed until next Monday.
items.explanation: The notice says 'Hot meals will not be available until Monday, but you can still buy sandwiches, cold drinks and ice creams'. The café is not closed, because the counter is still selling things, and the problem is a repair, not a lack of staff.

questions.question: Maria wants to read a true story about a journey. She reads on her phone on the train to work and would like something she can finish in a week or two.
questions.explanation: Walking Home is a 'true account' of a twelve-day walk, is 'only 150 pages long' and is 'an e-book, so you can download it straight to your phone'. Two Wheels, One World is also a true story about a journey, but it is 'over 600 pages' and 'only available as a large hardback', so Maria cannot read it on her phone.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Tom has just moved into his first flat and doesn't have much money for food. He wants to learn to make simple meals and likes to see pictures of how to do every stage.
questions.explanation: Cheap and Cheerful Cooking is for people 'cooking for themselves for the first time', has 'easy recipes' costing 'less than three pounds a portion' and 'photos showing each step'. From Garden to Table also has recipes, but they are 'impressive recipes for dinner parties' with ingredients 'from expensive food shops', and it has drawings, not step-by-step photos.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Hannah is fourteen and loves books that make her laugh. When she enjoys a book, she always wants to go on reading about the same characters in other books.
questions.explanation: Max Moves In is 'the funniest book' teenage readers have read this year, and 'it's the first in a series', with more books 'about Max and his cousin'. The Cat Who Solved Crimes is also 'very funny', but 'this will be the only book about Whiskers', so Hannah could not read more about the same characters.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: David drives a long way to work every day and would like to listen to a detective story in the car. He is especially interested in stories about the past.
questions.explanation: Murder at Kingsbridge Station is a 'detective novel' set in '1920s Manchester', with 'details of life a hundred years ago', and there is 'an excellent audiobook version' David can listen to while driving. The Cat Who Solved Crimes is also a detective story set in the past (Victorian London), but 'there is no audio version'.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Lucy lives in a flat with a small balcony and wants to grow her own vegetables. She has never done any gardening before.
questions.explanation: Small Space, Big Harvest shows how to grow vegetables 'in pots on a balcony or windowsill' and 'assumes you know nothing about plants'. From Garden to Table also explains how to grow vegetables, but 'in a large garden', and it is 'aimed at people with some experience', so it is wrong for Lucy.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.text:
Every Saturday morning, Leah Morgan, 26, takes her guitar and a small speaker to the square outside Bristol's main shopping centre. For the next four hours she sings to anyone who stops to listen. We asked her about life as a street musician.

How did you start?
'Almost by accident. I'd been playing in cafés for a couple of years, but they only paid me in free coffee! One day a friend dared me to play outside the railway station. I was terrified – my hands were shaking so much that I could hardly play the right notes. But a little girl stood in front of me and danced through every song, and by the end I'd completely forgotten my nerves. I went home with more money than I'd ever earned in a café.'

Is it hard work?
'People think we just turn up and play, but there's a lot more to it. In Bristol you need a permit from the city council, and there are rules about how loud you can be and how long you can stay in one place. I also check the weather forecast all the time. Rain is bad, obviously, but a very hot day is almost as bad, because people hurry from shop to shop and don't want to stand still.'

What's the best thing about it?
'The audience is completely honest. In a concert hall, people have paid for a ticket, so they stay even if they're bored. On the street, if you're not good enough, they simply walk away. That can be hard, but it has made me a much better performer. I've learnt to notice straight away when I'm losing people, and to change the song.'

Does anyone ever complain?
'Occasionally. A man who works in one of the shops used to come out and ask me to turn the music down. At first I was annoyed, but then I realised he had to listen to me all day. Now I play my quieter songs when I'm near his door, and he sometimes brings me a cup of tea!'

What are your plans?
'A few people have offered to manage me, and I've recorded some songs, which I sell as downloads. But I'm in no hurry to give up the street. I don't think I'd ever get the same feeling in a studio. Even if I become famous one day – which I doubt – I'd like to come back to the square now and then, just to remind myself where it all began.'

questions.question: What happened the first time Leah played outside the station?
questions.explanation: Leah was terrified at first, but 'a little girl stood in front of me and danced through every song, and by the end I'd completely forgotten my nerves'. She did not stop early, her friend only 'dared' her to play, and she earned 'more money than I'd ever earned in a café', not less.
options: a) Her friend had to help her when she made mistakes.
b) A child's reaction helped her to feel calmer.
c) She earned less money than she usually did in cafés.
d) She felt so nervous that she stopped early.

questions.question: What does Leah say about the weather?
questions.explanation: Leah says 'Rain is bad, obviously, but a very hot day is almost as bad', because people hurry and do not stop. She checks the forecast 'all the time' but never says she refuses to play, and the council rules she mentions are about volume and time, not rain. She does not say that sunny days bring more money; on very hot days people 'don't want to stand still'.
options: a) She never plays when the forecast is bad.
b) People give her more money when it is sunny.
c) The council does not allow street music in the rain.
d) Very hot days can be almost as bad as rain.

questions.question: Why does Leah think playing in the street has made her a better performer?
questions.explanation: Leah says street audiences are honest: 'if you're not good enough, they simply walk away', and 'it has made me a much better performer' because she notices 'when I'm losing people'. She never mentions advice from listeners, and there are rules about 'how loud you can be', so playing louder is not the reason.
options: a) People who stop often give her useful advice.
b) She has to perform for longer than in a concert hall.
c) People leave at once if they don't enjoy it.
d) She has learnt to play much more loudly.

questions.question: How did Leah deal with the complaints from the man in the shop?
questions.explanation: Leah understood that 'he had to listen to me all day', so 'Now I play my quieter songs when I'm near his door'. She still plays in the same square with her speaker, and she does not mention contacting the council about him.
options: a) She stopped using her speaker in the square.
b) She asked the council to speak to the man.
c) She moved to a different part of the square.
d) She changed the songs she played near his shop.

questions.question: What would Leah probably say about her future?
questions.explanation: Leah is 'in no hurry to give up the street', and even if she becomes famous she would 'like to come back to the square now and then'. She says she would not get 'the same feeling in a studio', and she doubts she will become famous ('which I doubt').
options: a) 'Whatever happens, I want to play in the street sometimes.'
b) 'I'm sure that I'll be really famous in a few years' time.'
c) 'As soon as I find a manager, I'll stop playing in the street.'
d) 'I'd much rather record music in a studio than play outside.'

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
Learning a new language as an adult can feel impossible. Three years ago I moved to Lisbon for work without knowing a single word of Portuguese. Today I can chat comfortably with my neighbours and even argue with the plumber. Here is what worked for me.

First, I stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend. (1) ______ Instead, I spent twenty minutes on Portuguese every single day, usually on the bus to work. Short, regular practice turned out to be far more effective than long, tiring sessions.

Second, I learnt the words I actually needed. Textbooks often begin with colours and animals, but I needed to buy bread, pay bills and ask for directions. (2) ______ That list became my first vocabulary book, and because I was using the words every day, I remembered them easily.

My third tip is to accept that you will make mistakes. For months I was so worried about saying something wrong that I hardly spoke at all. (3) ______ She told me that people would be pleased I was trying, and she was right. Most people I met were patient and helpful, and some even corrected me in a friendly way.

It also helps to bring the language into your free time. I changed the language on my phone to Portuguese and started watching films with Portuguese subtitles. (4) ______ After a while, though, I found I could follow a whole film without stopping it once.

Finally, find a reason to speak that has nothing to do with lessons. I joined a local running club, where nobody spoke English. (5) ______ Now some of those runners are my closest friends, and I no longer think about which language I'm speaking.

Learning a language takes time, and there is no magic method. But if you practise a little every day and don't give up, you will be surprised how far you can go.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
questions.explanation: The writer 'stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend'; the sentence about ending up 'tired and bored' and forgetting everything 'by Monday' gives the reason, and 'Instead, I spent twenty minutes... every single day' follows naturally. The sentence about preferring 'a grammar book on Sunday afternoons' is also about weekend study, but it contradicts the writer's decision to stop.
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
questions.explanation: The writer needed words for everyday tasks, not colours and animals, 'So I made a list of every phrase I needed'. The next sentence begins 'That list became my first vocabulary book', which refers back to this list. No other sentence mentions a list.
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
questions.explanation: The writer 'hardly spoke at all', so Rosa 'noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice'. The next sentence, 'She told me that people would be pleased I was trying', refers to Rosa and repeats her advice. No other sentence introduces a woman who could be 'she'.
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
questions.explanation: 'This' refers to watching films with Portuguese subtitles, which was 'very frustrating' because the writer had 'to pause every few minutes'. The next sentence contrasts with it: 'After a while, though, I found I could follow a whole film without stopping it once.' The sentence about being 'tired and bored' does not fit, because it talks about forgetting things 'by Monday', which only makes sense after weekend study.
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
questions.explanation: In the running club 'nobody spoke English', so at first the writer 'could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but 'gradually we started chatting on the long runs'. This leads to 'Now some of those runners are my closest friends'. The sentence saying 'everyone there spoke excellent English' contradicts the text.
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.

G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Twenty years ago, most people were nervous about buying things online. Today, millions of us (1) ______ our weekly shopping without leaving the house. But how do we decide what to buy?

Many shoppers spend a long time reading reviews by other customers before they (2) ______ a decision. A product with hundreds of positive comments is far more likely to sell than one with none, even if it is more expensive.

Price is still important. Lots of people (3) ______ prices on several websites to find the best deal, and some wait for the sales, when shops (4) ______ big discounts.

However, shopping online is not always as easy as it looks. Clothes may not fit, and colours often look different on a screen. That is why many companies now let customers send items back free of (5) ______.

Some experts believe that in the future we will do even more of our shopping online. Others think we will always want to see and touch things first. Whoever is right, one thing is (6) ______: the way we shop has changed for ever.

questions.question: Gap (1): millions of us ____ our weekly shopping without leaving the house.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'do the shopping' / 'do our weekly shopping'. We do not say 'make', 'take' or 'have' our shopping in English.
options: a) do
b) take
c) have
d) make

questions.question: Gap (2): before they ____ a decision.
questions.explanation: The collocation is 'make a decision'. 'Do a decision', 'put a decision' and 'get a decision' are not correct English.
options: a) get
b) make
c) do
d) put

questions.question: Gap (3): Lots of people ____ prices on several websites to find the best deal.
questions.explanation: To find the best deal, people look at the prices on different websites to see which is cheapest: they 'compare prices'. 'Compete' needs 'with' and is about trying to win, 'correct' means remove mistakes, and 'confuse prices' would not help anyone find a good deal.
options: a) correct
b) confuse
c) compete
d) compare

questions.question: Gap (4): when shops ____ big discounts.
questions.explanation: Shops 'offer discounts' to customers. Shops do not 'pay', 'spend' or 'earn' discounts; these verbs are used with money, not with discounts.
options: a) earn
b) offer
c) pay
d) spend

questions.question: Gap (5): let customers send items back free of ____.
questions.explanation: 'Free of charge' is a fixed expression meaning 'without paying'. 'Free of money', 'free of price' and 'free of value' are not used in English.
options: a) money
b) price
c) charge
d) value

questions.question: Gap (6): Whoever is right, one thing is ____: the way we shop has changed for ever.
questions.explanation: 'One thing is certain' means 'one thing is sure to be true'. 'Secure' and 'safe' describe things that are protected from danger, and 'confident' describes people, not facts.
options: a) certain
b) secure
c) safe
d) confident

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.textTitle: From a village to the city
lesenParts.text:
Last year I left my small village in Wales and moved to Manchester to start my first job. I had never lived anywhere bigger (1) ______ our local market town, so I was quite nervous.

At first, everything felt strange. I was afraid (2) ______ getting lost, so I carried a map everywhere, and at night the noise of the traffic kept me awake. I didn't know anyone in the city, and neither (3) ______ my flatmate, who had just arrived from Spain. We spent most evenings watching television in our tiny kitchen.

Things got better when I found (4) ______ about a climbing club near my office. We went along together one evening, and now we go twice a week. Most of our friends here are people we met on the climbing wall.

These days I really enjoy city life. (5) ______ is always something to do, from free concerts in the park to street markets at the weekend. Rents are expensive, and I sometimes miss the quiet countryside. At (6) ______ same time, I can't imagine going back now. Moving to Manchester was one of the best decisions of my life.

questions.question: Gap (1): I had never lived anywhere bigger ____ our local market town.
questions.explanation: 'Bigger' is a comparative adjective, so it must be followed by 'than' before the thing it is compared with ('our local market town'). No other word can link a comparative to its second part.

questions.question: Gap (2): I was afraid ____ getting lost, so I carried a map everywhere.
questions.explanation: The adjective 'afraid' is followed by the preposition 'of' + noun or -ing form ('afraid of getting lost'). 'About', 'for' or 'to' do not work before 'getting' here.

questions.question: Gap (3): I didn't know anyone in the city, and neither ____ my flatmate.
questions.explanation: 'Neither + auxiliary + subject' means 'also not'. The first verb is in the past simple negative ('didn't know'), so the auxiliary must be 'did'. 'Was' or 'had' do not match 'didn't know'.

questions.question: Gap (4): Things got better when I found ____ about a climbing club near my office.
questions.explanation: 'Find out (about something)' is a phrasal verb meaning 'discover information'. Without 'out', 'found about' is not correct English.

questions.question: Gap (5): ____ is always something to do, from free concerts in the park to street markets.
questions.explanation: 'There is' introduces something that exists: 'There is always something to do'. 'It is always something to do' is not correct, because 'it' needs something to refer back to.

questions.question: Gap (6): At ____ same time, I can't imagine going back now.
questions.explanation: 'At the same time' is a fixed expression meaning 'but also / however'. 'Same' always takes 'the' in this phrase; 'a same time' or 'this same time' are not used.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
horenParts.transcript:
Man: Would you like something to drink with your meal?
Woman: Yes, a fresh orange juice, please.
Man: I'm really sorry, but our juice machine isn't working today. We've only got apple juice in bottles.
Woman: Oh, I don't really like apple juice. I'll have a cup of tea, then. Actually, no, I'm so tired this morning. Could I have a coffee instead? A large one, please.
Man: Of course. Milk and sugar?
Woman: Just milk, thanks.

Man: Right, that's two large margherita pizzas. They're nine pounds each, so that comes to eighteen pounds.
Woman: Oh, isn't there a special offer on Tuesdays? The poster in the window says two pounds off.
Man: That's right, if you collect the order yourself.
Woman: Great. So that's sixteen pounds, then?
Man: Actually, it's two pounds off each pizza, not the whole order. So you only pay fourteen.
Woman: Even better! Here you are.
Man: Thanks. Enjoy your meal.

Mum: Hi, love. Did you manage to get everything on the list?
Girl: I think so. Here's the milk, and I got the big box of eggs, like you said.
Mum: Lovely, thanks. And the butter? I need it for the birthday cake this afternoon.
Girl: Oh no, I knew there was something. I was looking at the list on my phone and the battery died.
Mum: Never mind. Could you pop back to the shop for it? It's only five minutes away.
Girl: OK, I'll go now.

Man: Excuse me, are we too late for breakfast?
Woman: No, you're fine. From Monday to Friday we stop serving breakfast at eleven, but at weekends we carry on until half past eleven. And today's Saturday, so you've still got about twenty minutes.
Man: Oh, that's lucky.
Woman: Then we start the lunch menu at twelve o'clock, if you'd prefer something bigger.
Man: No, breakfast is perfect, thanks. Two full English, please.

Man: Shall we try that new Italian restaurant on the high street tonight?
Woman: I rang them this morning, actually. They're fully booked until Saturday.
Man: Oh, what a shame. Well, we could just cook something here instead.
Woman: There's nothing in the fridge, though, and I really don't want to go shopping now. What about the burger bar near the station? It's cheap, and you don't need to book.
Man: Good idea. I haven't been there for ages. Let's go at about seven.

Woman: That was delicious. What would you recommend for dessert?
Man: Well, the chocolate cake is the most popular, but to be honest it's quite heavy after a big meal like yours.
Woman: Mm, I am quite full. What about the fruit salad?
Man: It's fine, but it's nothing special. If I were you, I'd have the apple pie. Our chef makes it fresh every morning, and it comes with ice cream.
Woman: That sounds lovely. I'll try that, then.

Woman: Hi there, what can I get you?
Man: I was going to have the chicken salad, but it says on the board that it's finished.
Woman: Sorry, yes, we sold the last one about ten minutes ago. The soup of the day is still available, though. It's tomato, and it comes with fresh bread.
Man: Hmm, I had tomato soup at home last night, so I don't really fancy it again. I'll just have a cheese sandwich, please.
Woman: No problem. Brown or white bread?
Man: Brown, please.

questions.question: What time does the café stop serving breakfast today?
questions.explanation: Breakfast stops at eleven only from Monday to Friday; "at weekends we carry on until half past eleven" and today is Saturday. Twelve o'clock is when the lunch menu starts.

Woman: Are you taking that jacket back to the shop? I thought you loved it.
Man: I do. The colour's great, and it fits me perfectly.
Woman: So what's the problem? Did you decide it was too expensive?
Man: No, it was actually in the sale, so it was a real bargain. But look at this. The zip's broken already, and I've only worn it twice.
Woman: Oh, that's annoying. Have you still got the receipt?
Man: Yes, luckily. I'm hoping they'll just give me a new one.

Man: Have you been to the new shopping centre yet?
Woman: Yes, I went on Saturday. Everyone told me it would be really crowded, but actually it was fine. I didn't have to queue anywhere.
Man: And what are the shops like?
Woman: Well, that's the thing. They're the same big chain stores you find in every town. I was hoping for some smaller, independent places, you know, something a bit different. So it was a bit disappointing, really.
Man: What about parking? That's always a nightmare in town.
Woman: Oh, that was great. It's free for the first three hours, and there were loads of spaces.

Woman: Did you see the post office has changed its opening hours? It's open until seven on weekdays now.
Man: Yes, I saw the notice.
Woman: Were you surprised?
Man: Not really. People had been asking for longer hours for ages. But it makes such a difference to me. I could never get there before five because of work, so I had to send all my parcels on Saturdays, and the queue was always awful.
Woman: I thought you'd be annoyed, because it's closed on Saturday afternoons now.
Man: That doesn't matter to me any more. I can just go on my way home.

Man: I really need a haircut, but I hated what the last place did to me.
Woman: You should try Sam's on Bridge Street. I've been going there for years.
Man: Is it cheap?
Woman: Not especially. It's about the same as everywhere else. And you have to book at least a week ahead, because it's always busy.
Man: So why do you like it so much?
Woman: Because they actually listen to you. They ask exactly what you want before they start cutting, and you come out looking the way you asked. That's rare, believe me.

Woman: The Sunday market was much bigger than I expected, wasn't it?
Man: Yes, there were loads of stalls. The clothes were a bit disappointing, though. It was mostly cheap T-shirts.
Woman: Really? I didn't think so. I found a lovely wool scarf for five pounds. But the food stalls were amazing.
Man: Absolutely. They were the best thing there. That Thai curry I had was fantastic.
Woman: I know. I'd go back just for the food, to be honest.

Girl: Dad, could you give me a lift into town on Saturday morning?
Dad: What for? Is it for that new phone? You know it's cheaper if you buy it online.
Girl: I know, and I'm not going to buy it in the shop. I'll order it online when I get home. I just want to see it properly first, and hold it in my hand. It looks quite big in the photos, and I want to check it'll fit in my pocket.
Dad: That's sensible. OK, I'll drive you in after breakfast.

horenParts.transcript:
Presenter: And now some news for everyone who's planning to go to the Millbrook Summer Festival next weekend. As many of you know, for the last five years the festival has been held in the town square. This year, though, it's moving to Castle Park, because the organisers needed more space for all the new events.

The main stage won't be in the same place as before, either. Last year it was right next to the car park, and lots of people complained about the noise from the traffic. This time you'll find it next to the lake, which should be a lovely setting for the evening concerts.

There's plenty for younger visitors, too. Sadly, the painting competition won't be happening this year, but instead there's a cake decorating competition on Saturday afternoon for anyone under twelve. The winner gets a family ticket for next year's festival.

Now, a practical tip. There will only be a small number of chairs, and they're mainly for older visitors. So the organisers suggest that you bring a blanket to sit on. And please don't bring umbrellas, because they block the view for people behind you.

Tickets cost twelve pounds at the entrance, but if you buy them online before Thursday, you'll only pay eight pounds. Children under five get in free.

Finally, getting there. There's very little parking near Castle Park, and taxis will be expensive that weekend. So the best thing to do is to take the shuttle bus from the railway station. It runs every twenty minutes and it's free if you show your festival ticket.

So, that's everything for now. Have a great time at the festival!

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Lucy Grant, who has just been chosen for the national swimming team at the age of seventeen. Lucy, when did you first start swimming?
Lucy: I was seven. Everyone assumes I loved it from the very beginning, but actually I was terrified of putting my face in the water. My older brother was the keen one. I only went along because Mum didn't want to drive to the pool twice. The lessons themselves were fun, though. Our teacher turned everything into a game.

Interviewer: Now you train at five o'clock in the morning. That must be hard.
Lucy: People always say that's the worst part. And at first I hated hearing the alarm. But now I actually love it. The pool's really quiet, and I feel I've already achieved something before the day starts. My teachers used to ask if I fell asleep in class, but I'm more awake than anyone! What I find harder is the evenings, when my friends go out and I have to be in bed by nine.

Interviewer: You changed coaches two years ago. Why was that?
Lucy: My first coach was lovely, and she had loads of experience. The club was just round the corner from my house, too. But she mainly worked with sprinters, and I'd started to realise that I was better at longer races, like the eight hundred metres. So I joined a club that specialises in distance swimming. It means a longer journey, but it was the right decision.

Interviewer: Last year you didn't make the final at the national championships. How did you deal with that?
Lucy: Of course I was disappointed for a day or two. Some people said I'd been unlucky, because I had a cold that week, but that wasn't really it. When my coach and I watched the video, it was obvious that my starts were too slow. So we worked on them all winter. Looking back, it was the best thing that could have happened, because I'm much faster now.

Interviewer: You're quite popular on social media. How do you feel about that side of things?
Lucy: Some swimmers say it adds a lot of pressure, but I don't feel that at all. And I only post once a week, so it doesn't take up much time. The best thing is when girls send me messages saying they've joined a swimming club because they watched my videos. That makes it all worth it.

Interviewer: Finally, what advice would you give to young swimmers?
Lucy: Don't worry about finding the perfect club or buying expensive kit. And please don't compare yourself with other swimmers all the time. The most important thing is to make sure you're having fun. If you aren't enjoying it, you won't keep going when it gets difficult.
Interviewer: Lucy Grant, thank you very much.

schreibenParts.task:
You must answer this question. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Read this email from your English friend Sam and the notes you have made.

From: Sam
Subject: Your phone!

Hi,

Good news - I've found your phone! It was under the back seat of my car. You must have dropped it when I gave you a lift home from the cinema on Friday. [Note 1: Great! Thank Sam]

I can bring it round to your house, or you can come and pick it up from mine. Which would be better for you? [Note 2: Explain which and why]

I'm free on Saturday or Sunday this week. When shall we meet? [Note 3: Suggest a day and time]

By the way, how have you managed without your phone for the last few days? [Note 4: Tell Sam]

Sam

Write your email to Sam using all the notes.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2 - Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for young people.

Articles wanted!
Technology in my life
What piece of technology do you use most, and what do you use it for?
Could you live without it for a week? Why or why not?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question 3 - Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
The phone rang at midnight.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 1 - Interview

The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question with at least one or two full sentences.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. What time do you usually get up on a weekday?
3. Tell us about what you usually do in the evenings.
4. What do you enjoy doing at the weekend?
5. Do you prefer spending your free time at home or going out? Why?
6. Tell us about something you did in your free time last week.

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 2 - Photograph

Look at the photograph. It shows a group of people relaxing in a park on a sunny afternoon. In the front, a young family is having a picnic on a blanket under a large tree; a man is reading a book, and a little girl is eating a sandwich. Behind them, two teenagers are throwing a frisbee on the grass, and in the background an older woman is walking her dog along a path next to a small lake.

Tell us what you can see in the photograph. You have about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 3 - Collaborative task

I'm going to describe a situation to you. A group of friends has a free afternoon next Saturday. They want to do something together, but they don't have much money. Here are some things they could do.

go to the cinema
go for a bike ride in the countryside
play football or basketball in the park
cook a meal together at someone's house
visit a museum in the town centre

Talk together about the different things the friends could do, and say which would be the most enjoyable. Then decide which activity is the best for the group. You have about two or three minutes.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 4 - General conversation

Discuss these questions with your partner.

1. What free-time activities are popular with people of your age where you live?
2. Is there a free-time activity you don't enjoy? Why not?
3. Do you think people have less free time now than in the past? Why?
4. Would you like to try a new hobby? What would it be?
5. Is it better to spend free time with friends or on your own? Why?
